## Guided Tutorial 5.1: Merging Charles River Tables Using Lookup Functions

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will combine data from four Charles River tables, SalesOrderLine, SalesOrder, Customer, and Item, into a single analysis-ready dataset. This merged dataset will include the order date, the customer name, the customer region, the item name, the item group, the ordered quantity, the base list price, the standard cost, and a calculated extended amount for every order line. The result is the foundation for the customer profitability view described in the opening scenario.

**Prerequisites.** You need the Charles River Excel workbook open with the SalesOrderLine, SalesOrder, Customer, and Item worksheets converted to named Excel Tables, following the steps from Chapter 4. Throughout this tutorial, the ordered-quantity column on SalesOrderLine is referred to as QuantityOrdered. If your workbook labels that column differently, substitute the name your workbook uses.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1.** Click on the SalesOrderLine worksheet. This Table serves as the base for the merged dataset because it contains one row per order line, which is the level of detail needed for line-level profitability. You will add columns that pull information from the other three Tables using lookup functions.

**Step 2.** Click on the first empty column header to the right of the existing data. Type "OrderDate" as the column header and press Enter. In the first data row of this new column, enter the formula =XLOOKUP([@SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[OrderDate], "No Match") and press Enter. Excel fills the formula down the entire column automatically. This formula retrieves the order date from the SalesOrder Table by matching on SalesOrderID.

*[Figure 5.6: Screenshot of the SalesOrderLine Table with the new OrderDate column populated by the XLOOKUP formula. The formula bar shows the XLOOKUP syntax. Annotations identify the lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, and if_not_found components.]*

**Step 3.** Add another column with the header "CustomerID". Enter the formula =XLOOKUP([@SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[CustomerID], "No Match"). This retrieves the CustomerID associated with each order, which you will use in the next steps to look up the customer's name, region, and segment. Notice that the SalesOrderLine table does not store CustomerID directly, because a sales order line belongs to an order and the order belongs to a customer. The lookup bridges that gap.

**Step 4.** Add a column with the header "CustomerName". This requires a two-step lookup because the SalesOrderLine table carries SalesOrderID but not CustomerID, and the CustomerName lives in the Customer table. Enter the formula =XLOOKUP(XLOOKUP([@SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[SalesOrderID], SalesOrder[CustomerID]), Customer[CustomerID], Customer[CustomerName], "Unknown Customer"). The inner XLOOKUP retrieves the CustomerID for the current order, and the outer XLOOKUP uses that CustomerID to retrieve the customer name. This nested lookup traverses two tables in a single formula.

**Step 5.** Add a column with the header "Region". Because you added the CustomerID column in Step 3, you can now look up the region directly. Enter the formula =XLOOKUP([@CustomerID], Customer[CustomerID], Customer[Region], "Unknown"). Add one more column with the header "CustomerSegment" and the formula =XLOOKUP([@CustomerID], Customer[CustomerID], Customer[CustomerSegment], "Unknown"). The customer segment classifies each customer as Wholesale or Direct, which will matter for the disaggregated revenue analysis in Chapter 6.

*[Figure 5.7: Screenshot of the SalesOrderLine Table with all lookup columns populated, showing OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, Region, CustomerSegment, ItemName, and ItemGroup alongside the original SalesOrderLine fields. The formula bar displays the nested XLOOKUP for CustomerName.]*

**Step 6.** Add a column with the header "ItemName" and the formula =XLOOKUP([@ItemID], Item[ItemID], Item[ItemName], "Unknown Item"). Add a column with the header "ItemGroup" and the formula =XLOOKUP([@ItemID], Item[ItemID], Item[ItemGroup], "Unknown"). The item group classifies each item as Furniture, Lighting, Textiles, or Accessories. Add two more columns named "StandardCost" and "ListPrice" using =XLOOKUP([@ItemID], Item[ItemID], Item[StandardCost], 0) and =XLOOKUP([@ItemID], Item[ItemID], Item[ListPrice], 0). These cost and price values support the margin work in the end-of-chapter exercises.

**Step 7.** Add a calculated column with the header "ExtendedAmount" and the formula =[@QuantityOrdered]*[@BaseListPrice]. This computes the ordered value of each line from the ordered quantity and the base list price that the SalesOrderLine table records. The billed amount for each line eventually appears in the SalesInvoiceLine table as LineTotal once the order ships and is invoiced, and you will work with that billed figure in later chapters. For this ordered-stage profitability view, the extended amount is the appropriate measure.

**Step 8.** Verify the merged data by selecting a few rows at random and checking the results by hand. Pick a SalesOrderID, look it up in the SalesOrder Table to confirm the date and CustomerID, look up the CustomerID in the Customer Table to confirm the name and region, and look up the ItemID in the Item Table to confirm the item name. This manual verification step matters because lookup errors, such as a mismatched column reference or an incorrect Table name, produce results that look plausible but are wrong.

**Step 9.** Check for any "No Match", "Unknown", or "Unknown Customer" values in the lookup columns. Filter each lookup column and look for these indicators. If any appear, they signal a referential integrity problem where a foreign key in the SalesOrderLine or SalesOrder Table references an identifier that does not exist in the parent Table. Record the number of unmatched records for each column.

**Checkpoint.** Your SalesOrderLine Table should now contain the original line fields plus nine new columns, which are OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, Region, CustomerSegment, ItemName, ItemGroup, StandardCost, and ListPrice, along with the calculated ExtendedAmount. Every row should represent a single order line enriched with the date, customer, and item context needed for profitability analysis. If your lookup columns contain values rather than errors and your random checks confirm correct matches, this merged dataset is ready for the summarization and modeling techniques you will learn in Chapters 6 and 7.
